questions.scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent: you are building a support agent with the Claude Agent SDK. It handles returns, billing disputes and account issues through custom MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). The target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while still escalating the right cases.
questions.stem: A customer writes: "My blender arrived cracked. I don't want to go through a bot, just connect me to a real person." The order is in the system, the item is under warranty, and a replacement is something the agent could normally approve in one step. What should the agent do?

options.text: Run lookup_order first so it can offer an instant replacement, and escalate only if the customer still declines that offer after seeing it.
Call escalate_to_human right away, passing a short structured summary of what the customer already said (damaged blender, wants a person) so the human need not re-ask.
Acknowledge the frustration, explain that a replacement can be approved immediately, and escalate only if the customer repeats the request for a person.
Ask the customer to rate how urgent the issue feels on a short scale, and escalate to a human only when that rating is above the configured urgency threshold.

questions.explanation: An explicit request for a human is a valid escalation trigger on its own, and it should be **honored immediately**, without first investigating or trying to resolve the case. Because the human agent cannot see the transcript, the handoff should carry a compact structured summary of what is already known. Nothing in that summary requires a lookup the customer did not ask for.

whyWrong.A: Investigating and pitching a fix first overrides a clear, explicit preference. That the issue is easy to solve doesn't change what the customer asked for.
whyWrong.C: The "acknowledge and offer to resolve, escalate if they repeat" pattern applies to a *frustrated* customer who has **not** asked for a human. Here the request is already explicit.
whyWrong.D: Self-reported urgency is a sentiment-style proxy and isn't an escalation criterion. It also adds friction to a request that was already clear.

questions.mindset: An explicit request for a human is a trigger in itself: honor it now and hand off with context.

questions.stem: A support agent built on the Claude API gets this message: "THIS IS THE THIRD TIME my package is late!!! Ridiculous." The delivery-delay credit is fully covered by policy, and the agent has the tools to apply it. The customer has not asked for a person. Product owners want a high first-contact resolution rate without ignoring customer preferences. Which behavior is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Escalate to a human right away, because strong negative sentiment shows the case is too sensitive for an automated agent to handle well.
Apply the credit silently and close the case, since the issue is within policy and acknowledging emotions adds no value to the resolution.
Ask the model to rate its own confidence in handling an upset customer, and escalate whenever that self-rating falls below a fixed cut-off.
Acknowledge the frustration, offer to apply the delay credit now, and escalate only if the customer then says they would still prefer a person.

questions.explanation: Frustration on its own is not an escalation trigger. When the issue is within the agent's capability, the agent should **acknowledge the frustration and offer the resolution**, and escalate only if the customer restates that they want a human. This protects first-contact resolution and still respects the customer's choice.

whyWrong.A: Sentiment is an unreliable proxy for case complexity. Angry customers often have simple, solvable problems, so this pushes solvable cases to humans and lowers first-contact resolution.
whyWrong.B: This fixes the problem but ignores the customer's experience and gives them no chance to say what they prefer. The qualifier "without ignoring customer preferences" rules it out.
whyWrong.C: Self-reported confidence scores are poorly calibrated and don't track actual case complexity, so they make a weak routing signal.

questions.mindset: Sentiment is not complexity: resolve what you can, and escalate on criteria or an explicit request.

questions.scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent: you are building a support agent with the Claude Agent SDK. It handles returns, billing disputes and account issues through custom MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). The target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while still escalating the right cases.
questions.stem: A customer says, "I'm Maria Lopez and I was double-charged last month." get_customer with that name returns three active accounts in different cities. One of them has a recent duplicate charge on record. What is the MOST reliable next step?

options.text: Ask the customer for an additional identifier, such as the account email or an order number, and continue only after a single account matches.
Pick the account with the recent duplicate charge, since that best fits the complaint, and confirm the refund amount with the customer before processing.
Escalate to a human agent, because several matching accounts means the request is too ambiguous for the agent to handle on its own.
Refund the duplicate charge on the matching account and add a note to the other two accounts so staff can review them if needed.

questions.explanation: When a lookup returns **multiple matches**, the agent should **ask for an additional identifier** rather than choose one by heuristic. A wrong guess on a financial action affects the wrong person's account. A clarifying question is cheap and removes the ambiguity completely.

whyWrong.B: This is heuristic selection. "Best fit" is a guess. Another Maria Lopez could also have a duplicate charge, and confirming the amount doesn't confirm the identity.
whyWrong.C: Ambiguous identity is solvable with one question, so it isn't a policy gap or a dead end. Escalating here hurts first-contact resolution for no gain.
whyWrong.D: This takes a financial action on an account whose identity was never confirmed. Notes on the other accounts don't fix the risk.

questions.mindset: Ambiguous identity calls for a clarifying question, never a guess.

questions.scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent: you are building a support agent with the Claude Agent SDK. It handles returns, billing disputes and account issues through custom MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). The target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while still escalating the right cases.
questions.stem: Logs show the agent escalates many routine cases (standard damaged-item replacements with photo evidence attached). Yet it approved a competitor price-match request by itself, even though the written policy covers only price adjustments for your own store. You want better escalation calibration with the least added machinery. Which TWO changes should you make? Choose TWO.

options.text: Have the model output a confidence score with each reply, and route any reply scored below 0.7 to escalate_to_human automatically.
Add explicit escalation criteria to the system prompt, with few-shot examples contrasting cases to resolve directly and cases to escalate, each with its reasoning.
Train a separate classifier on historical tickets to predict escalation, and run it before the main agent sees each new conversation.
Add a sentiment-analysis step that escalates automatically whenever the customer's measured frustration score rises above a tuned threshold.
Define requests the written policy does not address, such as competitor price matching, as a policy-gap trigger the agent must escalate rather than decide.

questions.explanation: Mis-calibrated escalation is best fixed with **explicit criteria plus few-shot examples** showing when to escalate and when to resolve, including why. The second failure is a **policy gap**: when policy is silent or ambiguous about a request (competitor price matching when policy covers only own-store adjustments), the agent should escalate, not improvise. Both changes go after the root cause with minimal machinery.

whyWrong.A: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated. The agent is probably *confident* on the competitor case, so this wouldn't catch it.
whyWrong.C: A separate classifier is over-engineering when the agent simply lacks clear criteria. It also needs labeled data and upkeep. Try prompt-level criteria first.
whyWrong.D: Sentiment measures mood, not case complexity or policy coverage. It wouldn't stop the over-escalation of routine cases, and it wouldn't catch a calm competitor price-match request.

questions.mindset: Calibrate escalation with explicit criteria and examples; treat policy gaps as escalation triggers.

questions.stem: Which situation is, by itself, the strongest reason for a customer-facing agent to escalate to a human?

options.text: The case needs several tool calls across billing and order systems before a resolution can be worked out.
The customer's messages contain strong negative language and repeated complaints about earlier support contacts.
The customer asks for something the written policy does not cover, so no rule says whether it is allowed.
The model states that it is only moderately confident about the answer it is about to give the customer.

questions.explanation: Valid escalation triggers are an explicit request for a human, a **policy exception or gap** (the policy is silent or ambiguous), and an inability to make meaningful progress. Deciding an uncovered request is a business decision the agent isn't authorized to make.

whyWrong.A: Complexity alone isn't a trigger. Multi-step cases that stay within policy are exactly what an agent with tools should resolve.
whyWrong.B: Negative sentiment is an unreliable proxy for complexity. Acknowledge it and offer a resolution; escalate if the customer asks for a human.
whyWrong.D: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated, so it is a weak basis for escalation decisions.

questions.mindset: Escalate on policy gaps, explicit requests, or no progress, not on complexity, mood, or self-rated confidence.

questions.scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent: you are building a support agent with the Claude Agent SDK. It handles returns, billing disputes and account issues through custom MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). The target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while still escalating the right cases.
questions.stem: A customer insists order #A-7781 exists. lookup_order has returned "not found" three times, once each with the raw ID, without the prefix, and filtered by the customer's email. The customer has already re-read the order number and email from their receipt screenshot, and both match what the agent used. The agent has no other tool that can search orders. What should the agent do next?

options.text: Keep trying more ID formats and date ranges until the run reaches max_turns, since a match may still turn up with enough variations.
Tell the customer that the order does not exist in the system and ask them to contact the store where the purchase was made.
Ask the model to double-check its earlier tool calls and to state its confidence that the order is truly missing before replying.
Escalate to a human with a structured handoff: customer ID, the order number, the lookups already tried and their results, and a suggested next step.

questions.explanation: Being **unable to make meaningful progress** is a valid escalation trigger. The agent has used up its tools, and more retries won't change the result. The human taking over has no transcript, so the handoff should be **structured**: who the customer is, what was attempted, the results, and a recommended action. That avoids repeated work and a second round of questions to the customer.

whyWrong.A: Unbounded retries burn turns and the customer's patience without new information. max_turns is a safety net, not a strategy.
whyWrong.B: This treats "not found in our lookup" as proof that the order doesn't exist, which contradicts the receipt and leaves the customer stuck.
whyWrong.C: Self-checking doesn't add the missing capability. The agent still can't find the order, and a confidence statement doesn't decide anything.

questions.mindset: When the tools are exhausted, escalate with a structured handoff instead of looping or guessing.

questions.scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude: you are building an Agent SDK tool that helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases and understand legacy systems. It uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and some MCP servers.
questions.stem: An engineer has used the tool for about two hours to understand a legacy billing system. Early on, the agent found that invoices are built by `LedgerPostingService` and `InvoiceAssembler`. Now its answers are vague, saying things like "this probably follows a typical service-layer pattern," and some contradict its earlier findings. Which change MOST directly addresses this?

options.text: Move the session to a model with a larger context window, so the earlier discoveries stay inside the window for the rest of the exploration.
Add a system-prompt instruction telling the agent to be specific, to name concrete classes, and never to rely on generic architectural patterns.
Have the agent keep a scratchpad file of key findings (classes, file paths, relationships) and consult it before answering new questions.
Clear the conversation and restart the exploration from scratch whenever answers start to drift, so the context window is always fresh.

questions.explanation: Vague references to "typical patterns" and inconsistent answers are signs of **context degradation** in long sessions. Writing key findings to a **scratchpad file** keeps them outside the context window, so the agent can reload exact facts (names, paths) when it needs them instead of relying on diluted earlier context. This is the structured note-taking technique.

whyWrong.A: A bigger window postpones the problem but doesn't stop attention diluting over a long, noisy history. Curation beats raw capacity.
whyWrong.B: The agent isn't ignoring an instruction. It no longer holds the facts clearly. A prompt can't restore information that has degraded.
whyWrong.D: Restarting throws away everything learned and forces costly re-exploration. Without persisted notes, the drift simply returns.

questions.mindset: Persist findings outside the context window; don't count on long history to keep them sharp.

questions.scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude: you are building an Agent SDK tool that helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases and understand legacy systems. It uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and some MCP servers.
questions.stem: During the discovery phase, the main agent runs dozens of Grep and Glob searches. Their raw output (thousands of matching lines) fills its context, and later reasoning about the overall architecture gets worse. The engineer wants to keep the session going and keep high-level coordination in the main agent. Which TWO practices help MOST? Choose TWO.

options.text: Delegate focused questions (for example, "find all callers of the refund API") to a subagent that does the searching and returns only a concise summary.
Read every source file into the main context at the start, so later questions never need another search and nothing gets missed.
Raise the max_tokens value on each response, so the main agent has more room to write out its reasoning about the search results.
Use /compact, with focus instructions about what to keep, once verbose discovery output has filled much of the context.
Run /clear after every search, so each new question starts in an empty context free of earlier search output.

questions.explanation: **Subagent delegation** isolates verbose exploration: the subagent searches in its own fresh context and returns a distilled summary, so the main agent keeps the high-level picture. **/compact** summarizes the conversation so far to free space while continuing the same session, and focus instructions shape what the summary keeps. In an Agent SDK session, /compact is sent as a prompt in the same way and emits a `compact_boundary` system message.

whyWrong.B: Loading the whole codebase is the opposite of context management. It fills the window with mostly irrelevant content and makes attention dilution worse.
whyWrong.C: max_tokens limits output length. It doesn't reduce the amount of search output already in the input context.
whyWrong.E: /clear starts a new, empty conversation, which throws away the findings the engineer wants to keep building on.

questions.mindset: Isolate verbose work in subagents and compact what remains; never flood the coordinator.

questions.stem: A coordinator agent explores a large codebase in phases. Phase 1 maps the main modules and their entry points. In phase 2, it spawns standard (non-fork) subagents to trace specific flows, such as checkout and refunds. The phase-2 subagents keep re-discovering the module layout, which wastes tokens, and sometimes describe it differently from phase 1. What is the BEST fix?

options.text: Tell each phase-2 subagent in its prompt to "build on what was already learned in phase 1" before starting its own searches.
Have the coordinator write a concise summary of phase-1 findings and include it in the initial prompt of every phase-2 subagent it spawns.
Pass the full phase-1 transcript, including all raw search output, into each phase-2 subagent so that no detail is lost.
Drop the subagents and let the coordinator run phase 2 itself, since it already holds all of the phase-1 findings in its own context.

questions.explanation: A standard subagent starts with a **fresh, isolated context**. It sees only its delegation prompt, not the coordinator's history. The coordinator should **summarize key phase-1 findings and inject that summary** into each phase-2 subagent's initial context. That gives a shared, consistent baseline without importing verbose raw output.

whyWrong.A: The subagent can't see phase 1, so telling it to build on that work gives it nothing to build on.
whyWrong.C: Raw transcripts bring back exactly the verbose output that subagents are meant to isolate. This bloats every subagent's context and dilutes attention.
whyWrong.D: This gives up context isolation. The coordinator's context would fill with phase-2 search noise and degrade its high-level coordination.

questions.mindset: Subagents only know what you hand them: pass distilled summaries, not transcripts.

questions.stem: A multi-agent codebase-audit job runs for hours inside an ephemeral container. Only a mounted workspace directory survives a restart. After a crash at about 70% complete, the coordinator restarts every subagent from the beginning, repeating hours of finished work. What is the MOST reliable way to support resumption?

options.text: Have each agent export its progress and key findings to a known manifest file in the workspace, which the coordinator loads on restart and injects into the agent prompts.
Raise max_turns and the container timeout so that the entire audit can finish inside one uninterrupted run and resumption is never needed in practice.
Add a system-prompt instruction asking the coordinator to remember which subagents have finished and to skip any that are already done if the job is restarted.
Have the coordinator re-run every subagent after a crash, but enable prompt caching so that the repeated work costs much less than it did on the first run.

questions.explanation: Crash recovery needs **structured state persisted outside the model**, in a location that survives the failure. Each agent exports its state to a known place, and on resume the coordinator **loads the manifest and injects it** into the agents' prompts so that they continue rather than restart.

whyWrong.B: Longer limits make a crash less likely to interrupt the job, but they don't make recovery possible. Any crash still loses everything.
whyWrong.C: The model's memory lives in a context that the crash destroys. An instruction can't persist state across a restart.
whyWrong.D: Caching may lower the cost of repeated prefixes, but the job still redoes hours of work. It treats the symptom, not the missing state.

questions.mindset: Durable progress lives in files the coordinator can reload, not in the model's context.

questions.scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code: your team uses Claude Code for code generation, refactoring, debugging and documentation in a large monorepo, with CLAUDE.md files and custom slash commands already configured.
questions.stem: Early in a long Claude Code session exploring the monorepo, a developer typed a glossary into the chat that maps legacy abbreviations used across the whole repository to their meaning (for example, LPS = LedgerPostingService). After the context was compacted automatically, Claude started guessing what the abbreviations mean. She wants the glossary to be reliably available after every compaction in this session and in future sessions, without re-entering it. What should she do?

options.text: Paste the glossary back into the chat as the first message after each compaction, so that the new summary is refreshed with it.
Save the glossary as a CLAUDE.md inside the legacy/ directory, where many of the abbreviated classes live, so it loads alongside that code.
Add the glossary to the project-root CLAUDE.md, which Claude Code loads at the start of every session and re-injects from disk after compaction.
Run /compact with focus instructions to keep the glossary, before automatic compaction has a chance to run and summarize it away.

questions.explanation: Compaction replaces the conversation history with a structured summary, so anything that existed **only in the chat** can be paraphrased or dropped. The **project-root CLAUDE.md** lives outside the message history: Claude Code loads it at session start and **re-injects it from disk after compaction**. Information that must stay exact for the whole exploration, and for later sessions, belongs there.

whyWrong.A: This works only as long as someone remembers to do it, and the glossary is exposed to summarization again at the next compaction. It is a manual workaround, not a reliable fix, and it does nothing for future sessions.
whyWrong.B: A nested CLAUDE.md loads into the message history only when Claude reads files in that subdirectory, and compaction summarizes it away with everything else. The abbreviations are used across the whole repository, so questions about other areas would not trigger it.
whyWrong.D: A focused /compact keeps the glossary in this one summary, possibly paraphrased, but later compactions can still drop it and new sessions start without it.

questions.mindset: Context that must survive compaction and sessions goes in persistent files, not the chat history.

questions.stem: Midway through a long Claude Code session investigating a flaky test suite, `/context` shows the window is mostly full of earlier log and search output. The developer wants to continue the same investigation and keep its conclusions, such as which three tests are affected and the suspected race condition. Which command fits BEST?

options.text: /clear, which frees the context window so that the investigation can continue with more room available.
/compact with focus instructions, such as keeping the affected tests and the race-condition hypothesis.
/context all, which expands the usage breakdown and removes the largest items from the window.
/resume, which reloads an earlier conversation so the investigation can continue from a lighter state.

questions.explanation: `/compact [instructions]` frees context by **summarizing the conversation so far** and continuing the same session. Optional focus instructions control what the summary keeps. That fits continuing an investigation while keeping its conclusions.

whyWrong.A: /clear starts a **new conversation with empty context**. It doesn't carry the conclusions forward.
whyWrong.C: /context only visualizes usage and suggests optimizations. It doesn't remove anything from the window.
whyWrong.D: /resume switches to an earlier conversation. It doesn't shrink the current one, and it would drop the recent findings.

questions.mindset: Compact to continue with a summary; clear to start fresh.

questions.scenario: Multi-Agent Research System: a coordinator agent built with the Claude Agent SDK delegates to specialized subagents. One searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings and one generates the final report. The system must produce comprehensive, cited reports.
questions.stem: Reviewers find that the final reports contain accurate-sounding claims with no citations, or with citations that point to the wrong source. Traces show that the web-search subagent records URLs, but each hop after it (coordinator, then synthesis) forwards only prose summaries of the findings. Which TWO changes BEST preserve provenance end to end? Choose TWO.

options.text: Have the report subagent run a fresh web search after drafting, and attach the most relevant link it finds to each claim in the report.
Require the search and analysis subagents to return structured claim-to-source mappings: the claim, the source URL or document name, and the supporting excerpt.
Add an instruction to the synthesis prompt asking it to "always cite your sources" for every factual statement in the output it produces.
Pass those mappings through to synthesis unchanged and require it to keep and merge them when combining findings, so each merged claim still carries its sources.
Use a larger model for synthesis, so that it can recall where each finding came from more accurately across the merged inputs.

questions.explanation: Attribution is lost when findings are **compressed without claim-to-source mappings** at any hop. The fix is structural: upstream subagents emit **structured claim-source mappings** (URL or document, excerpt), the coordinator forwards them as data rather than prose, and the synthesis step **preserves and merges** them, so every claim in the report can be traced to its evidence.

whyWrong.A: Searching after the fact attaches *a* plausible link, not the source the claim actually came from. That makes misattribution worse.
whyWrong.C: The synthesis agent never receives the sources, so an instruction to cite them invites fabricated citations.
whyWrong.E: A larger model can't recall source data it was never given. The information was lost upstream.

questions.mindset: Provenance must travel as data through each hop; it can't be reconstructed at the end.

questions.stem: Two credible industry reports, both published in the same quarter, give different sizes for the same market: one says $4.1B and the other says $5.3B. The document-analysis step has to pass this finding on for synthesis into a decision memo. How should it handle the conflict?

options.text: Report the average of the two figures as a single estimate, and note in the output that it blends two credible sources to give a balanced view.
Keep the figure from the source with the stronger reputation, and drop the other one so that readers of the final memo are not confused by two numbers.
Pass on both figures, each attributed to its source and stated method, explicitly flagged as conflicting, and leave reconciliation to the coordinator.
Leave the market size out of the output entirely, since two conflicting figures mean that neither one can be trusted enough for a decision memo.

questions.explanation: When credible sources conflict, **keep both values with source attribution and annotate the conflict**, rather than choosing or blending arbitrarily. Keeping each source's method and characterization helps the coordinator (or a human) decide how to reconcile before synthesis.

whyWrong.A: Averaging invents a number that no source reports and hides real uncertainty from the decision-maker.
whyWrong.B: Choosing by reputation is arbitrary and silently drops credible evidence. The reader never learns that the figure is disputed.
whyWrong.D: Leaving the data out discards useful information. A clearly annotated range is more valuable than a gap.

questions.mindset: Annotate conflicts with attribution; don't average, pick, or hide them.

questions.scenario: Multi-Agent Research System: a coordinator agent built with the Claude Agent SDK delegates to specialized subagents. One searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings and one generates the final report. The system must produce comprehensive, cited reports.
questions.stem: The synthesis subagent often flags "contradictions" between sources. On review, many are not contradictions at all: one source reports 2021 adoption figures and another reports 2024 figures for the same metric. The subagents' structured outputs currently include the claim, value and source URL. What is the MOST effective fix?

options.text: Require each claim's structured output to also carry the publication date and the data-collection period, so synthesis can interpret differences over time correctly.
Instruct the synthesis subagent to prefer whichever figure looks newest when two values disagree, and to discard the other one as probably outdated.
Add several few-shot examples to the synthesis prompt showing real contradictions next to differences caused by time, so it learns to tell them apart.
Add a filter step that drops any source older than two years before synthesis, so that outdated figures never reach the synthesis subagent at all.

questions.explanation: Without dates, the synthesis agent **can't tell** a change over time from a disagreement. Requiring **publication and data-collection dates** in the structured outputs gives it the data it needs to interpret the values correctly. This is a schema-level fix at the source.

whyWrong.B: "Newest-looking" is a guess because the dates aren't in the data. It also throws away a valid historical data point.
whyWrong.C: Examples can't help the model make a distinction that depends on data it doesn't have. This is a classic "more few-shot" distractor.
whyWrong.D: The filter needs dates that the pipeline doesn't collect, and it discards trend data that may matter to the report.

questions.mindset: Give synthesis the metadata it needs; dates turn false contradictions into trends.

questions.scenario: Multi-Agent Research System: a coordinator agent built with the Claude Agent SDK delegates to specialized subagents. One searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings and one generates the final report. The system must produce comprehensive, cited reports.
questions.stem: Stakeholders say the generated reports read as uniformly confident: findings backed by many independent studies sit next to claims from a single contested paper, with the same tone. Quarterly revenue figures are also buried in prose paragraphs. Which TWO changes to the report structure BEST address this? Choose TWO.

options.text: Convert all content into one consistent bulleted format, so every finding is presented in the same way and is easy to scan.
Remove any finding that rests on fewer than two sources, so the report only contains claims that are settled and well supported.
Add separate sections for well-established findings and contested ones, keeping how each source characterized its result and its method.
Ask the synthesis model to give each paragraph a self-assessed confidence score from 1 to 10, shown next to the paragraph text.
Present each kind of content in a suitable form: financial figures as tables, news developments as prose, technical findings as structured lists.

questions.explanation: A good synthesis **separates well-established findings from contested ones** and keeps each source's characterization and method, so readers can judge the strength of the evidence. It also **presents content by type** (tables for financial data, prose for news, structured lists for technical findings) rather than forcing everything into one format.

whyWrong.A: A single uniform format is the anti-pattern here. Financial data loses its comparability when it isn't in a table.
whyWrong.B: Dropping thinly supported claims hides uncertainty instead of communicating it, and may remove important emerging findings.
whyWrong.D: Self-reported confidence scores are poorly calibrated and don't show the reader *why* a claim is contested.

questions.mindset: Make uncertainty visible in the structure, and fit the format to the content.

questions.scenario: Structured Data Extraction: you run a pipeline that extracts fields from unstructured business documents with Claude, validates the output against JSON schemas, and feeds the results to downstream systems.
questions.stem: A contract packet contains a master agreement and a later amendment. The extraction finds two different renewal dates, one in each document, and the amendment does not clearly say it supersedes the master agreement. The schema currently has a single required renewal_date string field. Which approach is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Keep the date from the amendment, since later documents usually override earlier ones, and record that choice in the extraction log for auditors.
Keep the field required, so the model is forced to commit to one date, and add a downstream validator that checks the date format.
Set renewal_date to null so that no possibly wrong value reaches downstream systems, and continue processing the rest of the packet normally.
Let the output carry both candidate dates, each with its source document and excerpt, plus a conflict flag that routes it to reconciliation or review.

questions.explanation: When sources in the input disagree and the documents don't settle which one wins, the extraction should **include both values with explicit source attribution and a conflict annotation**. That keeps the evidence and lets a downstream reconciliation step, or a human reviewer (contradictory source documents are a standard review-routing trigger), make the call.

whyWrong.A: "Later usually overrides" is a heuristic. The stem says the amendment doesn't clearly supersede the master agreement, so this could be silently wrong.
whyWrong.B: A required single-value field pushes the model to pick or invent a value. A format check can't catch a well-formed but wrong date.
whyWrong.C: A null loses both pieces of evidence and makes a conflict look like missing data, so the problem goes undetected.

questions.mindset: Represent conflicts explicitly in the data; don't let the schema force a silent choice.

questions.stem: An internal assistant answers employee questions using policy PDFs supplied in the request. Auditors require each answer to point to the exact passage in the supplied documents that supports it. The team wants a built-in API mechanism for this rather than custom parsing. What should they use?

options.text: Instruct the model to add a bracketed page number after each sentence, and parse those markers out of the response text.
Enable citations on the supplied document content blocks, so that responses return cited passages linked to the source documents.
Ask the model to list the documents it used at the end of each answer, and have a reviewer spot-check the listed sources.
Run a second model call that compares each answer with the documents and adds the most similar sentence as a source.

questions.explanation: Claude's **citations** feature, enabled on the document blocks you supply, returns responses whose claims are linked to the **specific cited passages** in those documents. That is the built-in way to make answers traceable to exact source text.

whyWrong.A: Markers the model writes in free text are not tied to the source text and can be wrong or invented. This is the custom parsing the team wanted to avoid.
whyWrong.C: A document-level list doesn't map claims to passages, and manual spot-checks don't meet a per-answer audit requirement.
whyWrong.D: This retrofits attribution by similarity, which can link a claim to text it didn't come from. It also adds a second call when a built-in feature already exists.

questions.mindset: Use built-in grounding with citations when claims must trace to exact source text.
